cards.front: How many /26 subnets fit in one /24?

items.prompt: Carve 10.0.0.0/16 into /24s. How many, and what is the range?

items.explain: First is 10.0.0.0/24, so the 5th increments the third octet to 4.
A /24 splits into 4 x /26; each block is 64 addresses.
The 5th /23 block: 0,1,2,3,4 -> third octet 8 and 9; network is the even one, 10.1.8.0/23.

items.explain: /16 into /20s: 2^(20-16) = 16 blocks, each 4096 addresses; third octet steps by 16.

items.prompt: How many /27 subnets fit in a /24?

Point-to-point link needs exactly 2 usable addresses.

handsOnLab.brief: Use Python's ipaddress module to carve subnets, size masks for host counts, and produce a written subnet plan for a small office network. You verify every hand calculation from the notes against a real tool.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: The plan's subnet list exactly matches the ipaddress module output, and every host-count requirement is met with the smallest possible prefix.
handsOnLab.deliverable: subnet-plan.txt containing the supernet, each carved subnet with network/broadcast/usable range, and the Python commands used.
steps: Open a terminal and verify Python: run python3 -c "import ipaddress; print(ipaddress.IPv4Network('10.0.0.0/16').num_addresses)".
Create the supernet object: python3 -c "import ipaddress; n = ipaddress.IPv4Network('192.168.10.0/24'); print(n.network_address, n.broadcast_address)".
Carve it into /26s in Python: list(ipaddress.IPv4Network('192.168.10.0/24').subnets(new_prefix=26)) and record all four.
For a 50-host requirement, compute the smallest prefix in Python: iterate prefixlen 32 down to 1 and find the largest prefixlen with num_addresses - 2 >= 50.
Repeat the sizing loop for 100, 12, and 500 hosts; record each chosen prefix.
Allocate with VLSM in Python: take 192.168.20.0/24, carve a /25 first, then take the remaining space and carve a /26 from 192.168.20.128/25.
Verify no overlap: build the full set and confirm each new subnet's overlaps() against the others returns False.
Write subnet-plan.txt: supernet at top, then each subnet with network address, broadcast, first/last usable, and usable count.
Add a summary line per requirement: hosts needed -> prefix chosen -> usable addresses -> waste.
Run python3 to re-derive the broadcast of each subnet and diff mentally against the plan.
Summarize in the plan why /26 (not /25) was chosen for the 50-host requirement.
Read the finished plan once end to end and confirm every number traces to a Python command above.
handsOnLab.title: Subnet planning with Python ipaddress

mockTask.explain: Each /26 holds 62 usable addresses, covering 50 with minimal waste; the three blocks are contiguous and non-overlapping.
mockTask.q: Panel question: the team needs three subnets of 50 hosts each from 192.168.0.0/24. Which allocation do you propose?

notes.body: An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number written as four decimal octets, e.g. 192.168.1.77. Each octet is 8 bits, so each ranges 0-255. The address is split into a network portion (which subnet) and a host portion (which device). Worked example: write 192.168.1.1 in binary per octet. 192 = 11000000, 168 = 10101000, 1 = 00000001, 1 = 00000001, giving 11000000.10101000.00000001.00000001. The dots are just human separators; routers see 32 bits. A common beginner error is treating 192.168.1.200 and 192.168.2.200 as near each other: the third octet differs, so they are in different /24 networks and cannot talk without a router. Always read an IPv4 address together with its mask; the address alone does not tell you the network boundary.
notes.title: IPv4 anatomy: 32 bits, four octets

notes.body: CIDR notation appends /n to the address, where n is the count of network bits (1s) in the mask. The mask is n one-bits followed by 32-n zero-bits. Worked example: /24 means 24 ones: 11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000 = 255.255.255.0. /16 gives 255.255.0.0. /20 is trickier: the first two octets are all ones (16 bits), plus 4 bits of the third octet: 11110000 = 128+64+32+16 = 240, so /20 = 255.255.240.0. Quick method: for the partial octet, take 256 minus 2^(8 - bits used). For /27, the last octet uses 3 bits: 256 - 2^5 = 256 - 32 = 224, so /27 = 255.255.255.224. Memorize the octet values for 1-8 bits: 128, 192, 224, 240, 248, 252, 254, 255. Larger n means a smaller network; /32 is a single host.
notes.title: CIDR notation and the mask

notes.body: From a prefix you derive five facts: network address, broadcast address, first usable, last usable, and usable host count. Usable hosts = 2^(32-n) - 2, subtracting the network and broadcast addresses. Worked example: 192.168.10.0/24. Total addresses: 2^8 = 256. Network: 192.168.10.0 (host bits all zero). Broadcast: 192.168.10.255 (host bits all one). First usable: 192.168.10.1. Last usable: 192.168.10.254. Usable count: 256 - 2 = 254. Second worked example: 10.0.5.0/24 gives network 10.0.5.0, broadcast 10.0.5.255, usable 10.0.5.1-10.0.5.254. For non-octet boundaries the same logic applies bit by bit: in 192.168.10.64/26 the block is 64 addresses, 64-127, so broadcast is 192.168.10.127 and usable is .65-.126. The -2 rule has two exceptions: /31 (RFC 3021, 2 usable, no broadcast) and /32 (1 host). Memorize the powers of two from 2^1 through 2^16; every subnet question is answered by them.
notes.title: Network, broadcast, and usable hosts

notes.body: Subnetting carves a larger network into smaller equal pieces by extending the prefix. The number of new subnets is 2^(new_prefix - old_prefix). Worked example: carve 10.0.0.0/16 into /24s. Count: 2^(24-16) = 2^8 = 256 subnets. The third octet runs 0-255: 10.0.0.0/24, 10.0.1.0/24, 10.0.2.0/24, up to 10.0.255.0/24. Each holds 254 usable hosts. The 5th /24 is 10.0.4.0/24 (count from zero: 0,1,2,3,4). Worked example 2: split 192.168.0.0/24 into /26s. Count: 2^(26-24) = 4. Each block is 64 addresses: 192.168.0.0/26 (0-63), 192.168.0.64/26 (64-127), 192.168.0.128/26 (128-191), 192.168.0.192/26 (192-255). Generalize: to carve, keep the network bits fixed and count the borrowed bits. This is the operation behind VPC subnet design: one large CIDR per environment, carved into tier subnets. When carving, always verify the first and last subnet addresses with a tool; off-by-one errors in the borrowed bits are the most common subnetting mistake.
notes.title: Carving subnets from a supernet

notes.body: Given a host count, find the smallest prefix whose usable addresses cover it: the smallest host-bits h with 2^h - 2 >= hosts, then prefix = 32 - h. Worked example: 500 hosts. Try h=8: 256-2=254, too small. h=9: 512-2=510 >= 500. So /23 (32-9), with 510 usable. Worked example: 60 hosts. h=5: 32-2=30, too small. h=6: 64-2=62 >= 60. So /26. Always round UP to the next power of two minus two; a /24 cannot hold 300 hosts (254 usable), you need a /23. Leave headroom: production subnets are usually sized one step larger than today's need because renumbering is painful. In cloud VPCs, remember the provider reserves a few addresses per subnet (AWS reserves 5), so size against usable-minus-reserved, not the raw formula.
notes.title: Sizing a mask for a host count

notes.body: VLSM (variable-length subnet masking) allocates different-sized subnets from one block to avoid waste. Worked example: from 192.168.10.0/24 serve needs of 100, 50, 25, and 12 hosts, largest first. 100 hosts need /25 (126 usable): take 192.168.10.0/25 (0-127). 50 hosts need /26 (62): take 192.168.10.128/26 (128-191). 25 hosts need /27 (30): take 192.168.10.192/27 (192-223). 12 hosts need /28 (14): take 192.168.10.224/28 (224-239). Addresses 240-255 remain free. Allocating largest-first prevents fragmentation. Supernetting is the reverse: summarize contiguous networks. Worked example: 192.168.0.0/24 and 192.168.1.0/24 share the first 23 bits (third octet 0 = 00000000, 1 = 00000001), so they summarize to 192.168.0.0/23. Route summarization keeps routing tables small, which is why ISPs and cloud route tables aggregate aggressively. Practice both directions until they are mechanical: given requirements, allocate with VLSM; given a set of routes, find the tightest summary.
notes.title: VLSM allocation and supernetting
